name: Croup
overview: Croup is a common childhood condition that affects the windpipe and airways, causing a distinctive barking cough. It is usually mild and gets better within 48 hours, but can sometimes make breathing difficult.
symptoms: A barking cough, often worse at night
A rasping sound when breathing in (stridor)
Cold-like symptoms such as a runny nose and high temperature
causes: Usually a viral infection, such as parainfluenza virus
Spread through coughs and sneezes
diagnosis: A doctor diagnoses croup from the typical cough and by examining the child's breathing.
treatment: Steroid medicine prescribed by a doctor to reduce swelling in the airways
Paracetamol or ibuprofen for fever or discomfort
Hospital treatment, including oxygen, for severe croup
selfCare: Keep your child calm and comfortable; crying can make it worse
Give plenty of fluids
Sit your child upright
Do not put a child in a steamy room or give them steam to breathe
whenToSeeDoctor: You think your child has croup
Symptoms are getting worse or lasting more than 48 hours
Your child has a high temperature or seems unwell
emergencySigns: Struggling to breathe, with the tummy sucking under the ribs
Lips or skin turning blue or grey
Unusually drowsy or floppy
Drooling or unable to swallow
Making a high-pitched noise when breathing at rest

name: Bronchiolitis
overview: Bronchiolitis is a common chest infection that affects babies and children under 2. It is usually mild and gets better within 2 to 3 weeks, but some babies need hospital care.
symptoms: Runny nose and cough at first
Feeding less and fewer wet nappies
causes: Viral infection, most commonly respiratory syncytial virus (RSV)
Spread through coughs, sneezes and touching contaminated surfaces
diagnosis: A GP diagnoses bronchiolitis from the symptoms and by listening to the chest.
treatment: Most babies get better at home with fluids and rest
Hospital care for breathing or feeding problems, including oxygen and fluids
Antibiotics are not used because it is caused by a virus
selfCare: Give small feeds more often
Use saline drops to ease a blocked nose if advised
Keep your baby upright
Keep your baby away from smoke
prevention: Keep babies away from people with colds
RSV immunisation for babies or in pregnancy where offered
whenToSeeDoctor: Your baby is feeding much less than usual
Fewer wet nappies
A high temperature
Your baby seems very tired or irritable
emergencySigns: Pauses in breathing
Struggling to breathe, with the tummy sucking under the ribs
Lips or tongue turning blue or grey
Your baby is floppy or not responding

name: Respiratory syncytial virus (RSV)
overview: RSV is a common virus that causes cough and cold symptoms. Most people recover within a few weeks, but it can cause serious breathing problems such as bronchiolitis and pneumonia in babies and older adults. Immunisations are available for some groups.
symptoms: In babies: wheezing, fast breathing and difficulty feeding
causes: Infection with respiratory syncytial virus
Spread through coughs, sneezes and touching contaminated surfaces
riskFactors: Babies, especially under 6 months or born prematurely
diagnosis: RSV is usually diagnosed from symptoms; a nose or throat swab test may be used in hospital.
treatment: Most people get better at home with rest and fluids
Paracetamol or ibuprofen for fever
Hospital care for breathing or feeding problems
selfCare: Rest and drink plenty of fluids
Wash hands often
Keep away from babies and frail older people while unwell
prevention: RSV vaccine in pregnancy and for older adults where offered
Catch coughs and sneezes in a tissue
whenToSeeDoctor: Symptoms getting worse
A baby is feeding less or has fewer wet nappies
You have a long-term condition and are worried
emergencySigns: Difficulty breathing or pauses in breathing
Lips or skin turning blue or grey
A baby who is floppy or unresponsive
Confusion in older adults

name: Scarlet fever
overview: Scarlet fever is a bacterial infection caused by group A streptococcus that mostly affects young children. It causes a rash and flu-like symptoms. It is easily treated with antibiotics.
symptoms: Flu-like symptoms such as high temperature, sore throat and swollen neck glands
A rash appearing 12 to 48 hours later, often starting on the chest and tummy, that feels like sandpaper
On darker skin the rash may be harder to see but still feels rough
A white coating on the tongue that peels, leaving it red and swollen ('strawberry tongue')
causes: Group A streptococcus bacteria
Spread through coughs, sneezes and touching contaminated surfaces
riskFactors: Close contact in schools and nurseries
diagnosis: A GP diagnoses scarlet fever from the symptoms and may take a throat swab.
treatment: Antibiotics prescribed by a doctor
Paracetamol or ibuprofen for fever and discomfort
selfCare: Drink plenty of fluids
Eat soft foods if the throat is sore
Use calamine lotion or antihistamines for itching
Stay off school or work until 24 hours after starting antibiotics
prevention: Do not share cutlery, cups or towels
whenToSeeDoctor: You think your child has scarlet fever
Your child is not getting better in a week, or has had chickenpox or measles recently
Your child is dehydrated
emergencySigns: Difficulty breathing, with the tummy sucking under the ribs
A child who is floppy, unresponsive or very drowsy
Blue lips or a rash that does not fade when a glass is pressed against it
Pauses in breathing

name: Roseola
overview: Roseola is a common illness in babies and young children. It causes a high temperature followed by a rash. It usually gets better on its own within a week.
symptoms: A sudden high temperature lasting a few days
A rash of small pink or red spots on the chest, tummy and back after the fever goes
causes: Infection with human herpesvirus 6 (HHV-6) or 7
Spread through saliva and droplets
diagnosis: A doctor diagnoses roseola from the pattern of fever followed by rash.
treatment: No specific treatment; it gets better on its own
Paracetamol or ibuprofen for fever
selfCare: Give plenty of fluids
Let your child rest
Keep your child away from others until the fever has gone
whenToSeeDoctor: Your child has a seizure for the first time
Fever lasts more than 5 days
Your child is not feeding or drinking well
Your child is under 3 months with a temperature of 38C or higher
emergencySigns: A rash that does not fade when a glass is pressed against it
A seizure lasting more than 5 minutes
Difficulty breathing
A child who is floppy or unresponsive

name: Slapped cheek syndrome
overview: Slapped cheek syndrome is a common viral infection in children that causes a bright red rash on the cheeks. It is usually mild and gets better on its own within 3 weeks. It can occasionally be more serious for pregnant people and people with some blood disorders.
symptoms: Mild cold-like symptoms such as high temperature, runny nose and sore throat
A bright red rash on both cheeks (may be less noticeable on darker skin)
A few days later, a spotty rash on the chest, arms and legs
causes: Infection with parvovirus B19
Spread through coughs and sneezes
diagnosis: A GP diagnoses slapped cheek syndrome from the typical rash; a blood test may be done in pregnancy.
treatment: No specific treatment; it gets better on its own
Paracetamol or ibuprofen for fever and joint pain
Antihistamines or emollients for itching
selfCare: Rest and drink plenty of fluids
Children can usually go to school once the rash appears, as they are no longer infectious
prevention: Pregnant people in contact with it should speak to a doctor
whenToSeeDoctor: You are pregnant and have been in contact with slapped cheek syndrome or have a rash
You have a blood disorder such as sickle cell disease or a weakened immune system
Symptoms are severe or not improving
emergencySigns: Very pale skin, breathlessness or fainting in someone with a blood disorder
A rash that does not fade when a glass is pressed against it

name: Hand, foot and mouth disease
overview: Hand, foot and mouth disease is a common infection in young children that causes mouth ulcers and spots on the hands and feet. It usually gets better on its own within 7 to 10 days. It is not related to foot and mouth disease in animals.
symptoms: A rash of spots or blisters on the hands, feet and sometimes the bottom or legs
Spots may be red, or darker or grey on darker skin
causes: Infection with enteroviruses such as coxsackievirus
Spread through coughs, sneezes, poo and fluid from blisters
diagnosis: It is diagnosed from the typical spots and mouth ulcers.
treatment: No specific treatment; it gets better on its own
Paracetamol or ibuprofen for pain and fever
Mouth gels or sprays for ulcers, as advised by a pharmacist
selfCare: Drink fluids, such as water or milk, to avoid dehydration
Eat soft foods and avoid hot, spicy or acidic food
Wash hands often
prevention: Wash hands with soap and water, especially after nappy changes and the toilet
Do not share towels or utensils
whenToSeeDoctor: Symptoms not improving after 10 days
Your child is not drinking or has fewer wet nappies
Your child has a weakened immune system
You are pregnant and have been in contact with it
emergencySigns: Your child is floppy, very drowsy or unresponsive
A stiff neck or seizures
Difficulty breathing

sources.label: NHS: Hand, foot and mouth disease

name: Head lice and nits
overview: Head lice are tiny insects that live in hair, and nits are their empty egg cases. They are very common in children and are not a sign of poor hygiene. They can be treated at home with wet combing or pharmacy treatments.
symptoms: Feeling like something is moving in the hair
Live lice in the hair, found by combing
Nits (empty egg cases) attached to hair close to the scalp
causes: Lice spreading by direct head-to-head contact
They cannot jump, fly or swim
diagnosis: Head lice are confirmed by finding live lice using a detection comb on wet or dry hair.
treatment: Wet combing with a special detection comb, repeated over 2 weeks
Lotions or sprays from a pharmacy
Treating everyone in the household found to have live lice on the same day
selfCare: Use conditioner and a fine-toothed comb to wet comb
Check the whole family
Repeat combing as instructed
prevention: There is no need to keep children off school
whenToSeeDoctor: Treatment has not worked after several attempts
The scalp is very sore or looks infected

name: Nappy rash
overview: Nappy rash is very common in babies and young children. It causes red, sore patches on the skin in the nappy area. It can usually be treated at home with simple care and barrier creams.
symptoms: Red or darker patches on the bottom or genital area
causes: Skin in contact with wee or poo for a long time
Rubbing from the nappy
Soaps, bubble bath or wipes that irritate the skin
A fungal (thrush) infection in some cases
diagnosis: Nappy rash is recognised by looking at the skin; a GP or health visitor can check whether an infection is present.
treatment: Barrier cream applied at each nappy change
Antifungal cream if thrush is suspected, as advised by a pharmacist or GP
selfCare: Change nappies as soon as they are wet or dirty
Clean with water or fragrance-free wipes
Leave the nappy off for a while each day
Pat skin dry rather than rubbing
whenToSeeDoctor: The rash does not improve after a week of treatment
Your baby has a high temperature
The rash spreads or looks infected, with blisters or pus
emergencySigns: A rash that does not fade when a glass is pressed against it
Your baby is floppy, very drowsy or not feeding

name: Febrile seizures
overview: Febrile seizures are fits that can happen when a child has a high temperature. They are frightening to see but are usually harmless and most children recover fully. They are most common between 6 months and 3 years.
symptoms: Body becoming stiff and arms and legs twitching
Sleepiness for up to an hour afterwards
causes: A rapid rise in temperature during an infection such as a cold, flu, ear infection or chickenpox
Rarely, after some vaccinations
diagnosis: A doctor diagnoses a febrile seizure from the description and checks for the cause of the fever.
treatment: Most stop on their own without treatment
Treatment of the underlying infection
Hospital care for long or repeated seizures
selfCare: During a seizure, place your child on their side on a soft surface
Do not put anything in their mouth
Time the seizure
Stay with your child
prevention: There is no reliable way to prevent febrile seizures; fever medicines make children more comfortable but do not prevent seizures
whenToSeeDoctor: After any first febrile seizure, even if it stopped
Your child seems unwell after a seizure
emergencySigns: A seizure lasting more than 5 minutes
First-ever seizure
Difficulty breathing or not waking up afterwards
Another seizure soon after the first
Signs of meningitis such as a rash that does not fade or a stiff neck

name: Glue ear
overview: Glue ear is when the middle part of the ear fills with sticky fluid, which can affect hearing. It is common in young children and usually clears up on its own within 3 months.
symptoms: Hearing loss: turning up the TV, mishearing or not responding
Ringing or buzzing in the ears
causes: Fluid build-up in the middle ear, often after a cold or ear infection
The tube linking the ear and throat not draining properly
diagnosis: A GP looks in the ear and may refer for hearing tests.
treatment: Watchful waiting, as it often clears within 3 months
Grommets (small tubes) inserted in the eardrum if it persists
Hearing aids in some cases
Antibiotics are not usually helpful
selfCare: Speak clearly and face your child when talking
Reduce background noise
Tell the school or nursery
whenToSeeDoctor: You think your child has hearing problems
Speech or behaviour concerns
Ear pain or discharge
emergencySigns: Swelling or redness behind the ear with fever
Severe headache, stiff neck or drowsiness

name: Threadworms
overview: Threadworms are tiny worms in poo. They are common in children and spread easily. They can be treated with medicine from a pharmacy and strict hygiene.
symptoms: Extreme itching around the bottom, especially at night
Seeing small white worms in poo or around the bottom
Itching around the vagina in girls
causes: Swallowing threadworm eggs, which are passed from fingers to the mouth
Eggs can survive on surfaces, bedding and clothes for up to 2 weeks
riskFactors: Living with someone who has threadworms
diagnosis: Threadworms are usually diagnosed by seeing the worms; occasionally a sticky tape test around the bottom is used.
treatment: Medicine from a pharmacy for everyone in the household
Strict hygiene measures for 2 weeks
selfCare: Wash hands and scrub under nails, especially before eating and after the toilet
Bath or shower every morning
Wash bedding, towels and soft toys
Keep nails short and discourage scratching
whenToSeeDoctor: Your child is under 2
You are pregnant or breastfeeding
Treatment has not worked
